html:
London at the centre is the chart's name for the long period, roughly 1783 to 1929, when London was the centre of the world economy, of its trade, shipping and finance. For Fernand Braudel it marks a change of kind: the first time the centre was a whole national economy, not a single city state like Venice or Amsterdam.

The start date is the peace of 1783 that ended the American war. Britain had lost its thirteen colonies, but by then it had beaten the Dutch at sea and its home market, tied together by roads, canals and London's demand, was the largest in Europe. Industry was beginning to take off.

What carried London:

  • British industry, from cotton mills to steam engines and railways, which sold to the whole world.
  • The Bank of England and the gold standard, which made the pound the world's money.
  • The City of London's banks, insurers such as Lloyd's, and its bill market, which financed trade between other countries too.
  • The Royal Navy and an empire that, under Victoria, spread over every continent.
  • London itself, the largest city in the world for much of the 1800s.

From the 1870s the United States and Germany caught up in industry. The First World War cost Britain heavily, and New York became a lender to the world. The end date is the Wall Street Crash of 1929. After that, and above all after 1945, the centre moved to New York.
